text: When something upsets you at school or work, what do you usually do first?
source: Yale Center for Emotional Intelligence — RULER Framework (Recognizing, Understanding, Labeling, Expressing, Regulating emotions)

options.label: I act out or shut down right away
I wait, but I'm still upset for a long time
I name the feeling and take a few breaths
I identify the feeling, think it through, and respond calmly

text: How well can you tell the difference between feeling nervous and feeling excited?
source: Yale Center for Emotional Intelligence — RULER Framework: Labeling emotions with precision improves regulation and decision-making across development.

options.label: They feel the same to me — I can't tell them apart
I know they're different but I mix them up often
I can usually tell which one I'm feeling
I can clearly name both and know what's causing each

text: After a difficult day, how do you recover before the next one?
source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child — Working Paper: Supportive Relationships and Active Skill-Building Strengthen the Foundations of Resilience (2015).

options.label: I usually carry it into the next day
I distract myself but don't really process it
I talk to someone or do something that helps me reset
I reflect on what happened, learn from it, and genuinely move on

text: When a friend or coworker is upset, how do you usually respond?
source: Yale Center for Emotional Intelligence — RULER Framework: Empathy and social-emotional skills are cornerstones of collaborative readiness.

options.label: I don't really notice or I walk away
I notice but I'm not sure what to do
I acknowledge how they feel and ask if they need something
I listen fully, reflect back what I hear, and offer genuine support

text: How long can you focus on one task — like reading, building, or solving a problem — without stopping?
source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child — InBrief: Executive Function and Self-Regulation. Sustained attention is a core component of developing executive function.

options.label: About 5 minutes or less
Around 10–15 minutes
30–45 minutes with a short break
Over an hour, adjusting breaks as needed

text: If your plan isn't working, how do you respond?
source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child — InBrief: Executive Function and Self-Regulation. Cognitive flexibility is the ability to shift strategies in response to new information.

options.label: I get frustrated and usually give up
I keep trying the same approach hoping it changes
I try a different approach after a while
I quickly assess what isn't working and deliberately try something new

text: When you're given a multi-step task, what do you do before starting?
source: Princeton Neuroscience Institute — Research on prefrontal cortex development: planning and working memory mature throughout adolescence and into the mid-20s.

options.label: I dive straight in without thinking about steps
I think about it briefly but don't write anything down
I make a rough list of steps before I begin
I break it into ordered steps, estimate time, and check for blockers first

text: How do you handle being asked to do something new that you've never tried before?
source: Princeton Neuroscience Institute — Adolescent brain research on novelty processing and cognitive readiness for unfamiliar task demands.

options.label: I refuse or freeze — new things feel too hard
I try but get overwhelmed quickly
I ask questions to understand it before trying
I welcome it, gather what I need to know, and give it a confident attempt

text: When working in a group, what role do you naturally take on?
source: Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health — Research on adolescent social development and cooperative learning environments.

options.label: I usually stay quiet and let others lead
I follow along and do what I'm told
I contribute ideas and help keep the group on track
I actively read the room, share leadership, and lift others up

text: When you disagree with someone in authority — a teacher, supervisor, or parent — what do you do?
source: Cornell ILR School — Research on adolescent workplace communication norms and authority relationships in early employment settings.

options.label: I say nothing or I argue back immediately
I feel frustrated but just go along with it
I wait for a calm moment and express my view respectfully
I listen first, then raise my concern clearly and constructively at the right time

text: How comfortable are you asking for help when you're stuck on something?
source: Yale Center for Emotional Intelligence — RULER Framework: Help-seeking is linked to emotional awareness and trust in social relationships.

options.label: I'd rather struggle alone than ask for help
I ask only as a last resort and feel embarrassed doing it
I'm mostly comfortable asking trusted people for help
I ask for help early, choose the right person, and learn from the interaction

text: How do you handle it when plans change unexpectedly and you have to adjust with others?
source: Princeton Neuroscience Institute — Social cognition research on flexibility and interpersonal adaptation across adolescent development.

options.label: I get upset and find it hard to move on
I go along with it but I'm annoyed
I adjust without much trouble
I help others adapt too and look for the opportunity in the change

text: How well do you manage your energy throughout a full day of activity or work?
source: Cornell ILR School — Occupational health research on physical endurance benchmarks and safe workload thresholds for adolescent workers.

options.label: I feel drained after just an hour or two
I manage but need several long rests to get through the day
I stay steady most of the day with normal breaks
I manage my energy proactively — I pace myself and finish strong

text: How do you respond to physically uncomfortable conditions — like standing for a long time, working in heat, or doing repetitive tasks?
source: Cornell ILR School — ILR School research on musculoskeletal risk and age-appropriate physical work demands for adolescents and young adults.

options.label: I can't handle it — I need to stop right away
I push through but complain or lose focus
I manage it without it affecting my performance much
I adapt my technique or posture and stay effective throughout

text: How well do you take care of your body to support your daily activities — sleep, food, exercise?
source: Harvard Center on the Developing Child — Working Paper: Early Childhood Program Effectiveness. Physical self-regulation and health habits are foundational to work readiness.

options.label: I don't really think about it — I eat and sleep whenever
I know it matters but my habits are inconsistent
I usually sleep enough and eat reasonably well
I actively manage sleep, nutrition, and movement as part of my routine
